title: Topological states of generalized dissipative Majorana wires
abstract: We study the generalized one-dimensional (1D) quantum dissipative models corresponding to a Majorana wire which can possess more than one Majorana bound state at each end. The system consists of a 1D fermionic open quantum system whose dynamics is governed by a quadratic Lindblad equation. Using the adjoint Lindblad equation for the fermionic two-point correlations, we find the gaps in the damping and purity spectra of a generic 1D model. Then, using the symmetry-based classification, we show that a winding number as the topological invariant can be defined which distinguishes different steady states of the system in the presence of damping and purity gaps. Then we focus on certain models with different Lindblad quantum jump terms and explore their phase diagrams by calculating the damping and the purity gaps as well as the winding number. In particular, we show that by inclusion of quantum jumps between next-nearest-neighbor sites, higher winding numbers and, equivalently, more Majorana bound states can be achieved. Also, by introducing imbalanced couplings, we can switch between states with negative and positive winding numbers. Finally, we should mention that since our formulation is based on the fermionic correlations rather than the Majorana operators, it can be easily extended to the dissipative topological phases belonging to other symmetry classes.
summary: This paper analyzes the topology of generalized dissipative Majorana wires using a Lindblad master equation framework. By calculating spectral gaps and defining a winding number invariant, the authors show that this topology persists even with damping. They demonstrate that engineering couplings allows control over the topological state, achieving higher bound states than simpler models.
main_problem: The study investigates topological states within generalized one-dimensional (1D) quantum dissipative models, specifically those modeling Majorana wires that can host multiple bound states.
main_result: The authors demonstrate that a winding number serves as a robust topological invariant distinguishing steady states even when damping and purity gaps are present. Furthermore, incorporating next-nearest-neighbor couplings allows for achieving higher winding numbers.
method: The analysis utilizes the adjoint Lindblad equation applied to fermionic two-point correlations, calculating spectral gaps (damping and purity) and defining topology via a symmetry-based winding number calculation.
model_or_system: The system is modeled as a 1D fermionic open quantum system whose dynamics are governed by a quadratic Lindblad equation. The model generalizes the Kitaev chain by including imbalanced couplings and next-nearest-neighbor interactions.

main_assumptions: The analysis relies on transforming to a mean-field description using phase-conserving linear operators and analyzing steady states derived from fermionic correlations rather than direct Majorana operator evolution.

paper_structure: The paper progresses by establishing the mathematical framework using Lindblad dynamics for fermionic correlations, deriving the topological invariant (winding number), and then applying this analysis to specific generalized models (Model I and Model II) to map out their phase diagrams.
why_interesting: This work bridges non-equilibrium quantum dynamics (Lindblad equations) with topological concepts typically associated with Hermitian Hamiltonians. The ability to define robust topological invariants in the presence of dissipation is highly relevant for understanding open quantum systems.

FIG. 2. (a) Dissipative (damping) gap of the Kitaev model with imbalanced coupling as a function of the imbalance con- trol parameter θ and the onsite dissipation parameter κ. (b) The topological winding number variation with the two pa- rameters θ and κ. As the model has always a nonvanishing purity gap, the change in the winding number exactly coin- cides with the dissipative gap closing lines. The switching between ν = ±2 has been made possible by the imbalanced coupling controlled by θ.

FIG. 3. (a) Dissipative (damping) gap and (b) the topolog- ical winding number of the Kitaev model, including n.n.n. coupling, as functions of the onsite dissipation parameter κ and the relative strength of n.n.n. coupling represented as β. Again and similar to the model with only n.n. coupling, the change in the winding number exactly coincides with the dissipative gap closing lines. For a large enough n.n.n. cou- pling (|β| > 0.5), we can achieve a higher value of topological invariant, which is ν = 4 for this model.
